rst31-hygiene2-noro-source-scope.title: Do not confuse the scope of “about eight-tenths”
rst31-hygiene2-noro-source-scope.text: The textbook’s “about 80%” does not mean that 80% of food handlers are infected. A similar explanation appears in MHLW’s 10 November 2017 notice, concerning norovirus food poisoning and food contamination via cooking workers. The textbook’s original statistical dataset has not been established, so do not substitute current all-food-poisoning or individual-store proportions. Explain continued contamination prevention through pre-work health checks and appropriate handwashing.

rst31-hygiene2-q049.explanation: The scope is norovirus food poisoning and contamination via workers, not worker infection prevalence or all-food-poisoning causes, nor a guarantee for current individual stores.

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q006.explanation: These are examples of foods with heating and cooling. Follow actual processes rather than fixing the category by name alone.
reasons: The name does not justify skipping cooling
Do not erase the heating step
Reheating does not replace checking cooling
It controls both actual processes

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q007.objective: Record daily heating results and abnormalities.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q007.stem: Heating work has finished for the day. Which record fits the source example?
options: Record the daily heating result and abnormalities, and follow additional shop requirements
Ignore individual shop records because the source gives an example
Record no abnormalities
Omit the daily result if appearance was normal
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q007.explanation: The example requires the final daily result and details of problems. Additional shop recording requirements still apply.
reasons: It satisfies both the example and shop requirements
The example does not cancel additional requirements
Abnormalities must also be recorded
Keep the daily result

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q008.objective: Prepare raw seafood and prevent foreign objects.
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q008.stem: Which approach correctly combines raw-seafood preparation and foreign-object prevention?
options: Inspect only at delivery, never during preparation
Seawater soaking eliminates all hazards
Wash in suitable fresh water, remove contamination concerns, inspect ingredients and work, and keep order
Tidying removes the need for washing and removal
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-q008.explanation: Use suitable fresh-water washing and removal for raw seafood. Ingredient and in-process checks plus order reduce foreign-object routes.
reasons: Objects can enter during preparation
Seawater alone cannot eliminate every hazard
It combines preparation and continuing prevention
Order does not replace required washing or removal

rst31-v2-r2-hyg-a-group3.title: From food names to process history
rst31-v2-r2-hyg-a-group3.text: If sauce was cooked and cooled yesterday, do not classify it only by how it is served today. Curry, soup, sauce, dipping sauce and potato salad are source examples of foods involving heating and cooling. Write down each actual process and control cooling after heating. The same name can require different controls when preparation differs.

rst31-v2-r2-cook-q001.objective: Remove unwanted parts and cut for the dish.
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q001.stem: Which preparation shapes an ingredient for the dish?
options: Peeling makes cutting unrelated to the dish
Always keep inedible parts
Use the same size for every dish
Remove unwanted parts and peel as needed, then cut to an edible, suitable shape
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q001.explanation: Preparation includes removal, peeling and cutting suited to the dish.
reasons: Peeling and suitable cutting require separate checks
Keeping unwanted parts is not the purpose
Required shape and size depend on the dish
It matches removal and cutting to the purpose

rst31-v2-r2-cook-q002.objective: Prepare ingredients promptly after refrigerated storage.
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q002.stem: The required ingredients have been taken from the refrigerator. What next?
options: Proceed promptly with preparation and avoid unnecessary standing
Leave them at room temperature for a long time
Ignore time if appearance is normal
Take everything out early and leave it if busy
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q002.explanation: Prepare removed ingredients promptly. Appearance alone is insufficient; prevent bacterial growth during work.
reasons: It avoids unnecessary standing through prompt preparation
Long standing conflicts with prompt work
Normal appearance does not remove time control
Plan quantity and progress without increasing standing time

rst31-v2-r2-cook-q003.objective: Distinguish washing ingredients from necessary disinfection.
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q003.stem: Which preparation reduces mud, dirt, microbes and foreign objects on ingredients?
options: Check smell without washing
Do not inspect ingredients because utensils were washed
Water alone always makes everything sterile
Wash appropriately and disinfect by the specified method when necessary
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q003.explanation: Wash ingredients properly and use specified disinfection when necessary. Washing and disinfection are different.
reasons: Smell does not replace washing
Utensils and ingredients each need appropriate handling
Water alone does not guarantee sterility
It distinguishes washing from required disinfection

rst31-v2-r2-cook-q004.objective: Choose suitable thawing that prevents bacterial growth.
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q004.stem: How should frozen ingredients be thawed according to the source?
options: Prevent growth and choose food-suitable methods such as refrigerator or running-water thawing
Prefer long standing in a warm place
Assume bacteria cannot grow during thawing
Choose from outer color alone
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q004.explanation: Prevent growth during thawing. Refrigerator and running water are examples; check conditions suitable for the food.
reasons: It connects growth prevention with a suitable method
Do not prefer long warm standing
Time and temperature matter during thawing
Color alone cannot identify a suitable method

rst31-v2-r2-cook-q005.objective: Separate one worker’s preparation, cooking and plating.
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q005.stem: Work surfaces are separated by use. May one person prepare raw ingredients, cook and plate at the same time?
options: Yes, if gloves are worn
Do not work simultaneously; finish each task and verify cleanliness before switching
Yes, if the surfaces differ
Yes, if no dirt is visible
rst31-v2-r2-cook-q005.explanation: Separate the person’s tasks as well as surfaces to prevent contamination between raw ingredients and finished food.
reasons: Gloves do not replace task separation
It avoids simultaneous work and enables a clean switch
Separate surfaces alone do not permit simultaneous work
Visible dirt alone is insufficient

rst31-v2-r2-svc-q001.objective: Recognize things that do not belong in food.
rst31-v2-r2-svc-q001.stem: A piece of paper is found in a dish. Which view of a foreign object is correct?
options: It is not a foreign object without an injury
Only metal can be a foreign object
Soft items are not foreign objects
Check it as a foreign object because it does not belong in the food
rst31-v2-r2-svc-q001.explanation: Foreign objects should not be in that food. Hardness or whether injury occurred does not alone decide the definition.
reasons: Treat it as foreign before injury occurs
Paper and other nonmetals are also included
Soft foreign objects also exist
It meets the definition of not belonging in the food

rst31-v2-r2-svc-q002.objective: Distinguish hard and soft foreign-object examples.
rst31-v2-r2-svc-q002.stem: Which grouping fits the source examples for an inspection list?
options: Everything is hard, so no soft category is needed
Everything is soft, so injury risk can be ignored
Stone, metal, glass and hard plastic are hard; insects, hair, vinyl and paper are soft
Stone and metal are soft; hair and paper are hard
rst31-v2-r2-svc-q002.explanation: The examples distinguish hard and soft objects. Softness does not remove the need to respond to contamination.
reasons: Soft examples also need classification
It ignores hard objects and injury risk
Both sets of representative examples are correctly matched
It reverses hard and soft examples

rst31-v2-r2-svc-q003.objective: Reconsider person, place and timing in difficult complaints.
rst31-v2-r2-svc-q003.stem: Strong dissatisfaction remains despite responding with the manager. What should be considered?
options: Time always solves it, so stop reporting
Changing location removes the need to check the complaint
Consider changing the person, place or timing and apologize again at departure if needed
Only repeat the same explanation louder
rst31-v2-r2-svc-q003.explanation: Reconsider the response with the manager when one method fails. Changes do not replace checking the issue or needed apologies.
reasons: Do not assume time always resolves it
The complaint still needs checking after moving
It considers response options and needed apologies
Repeating loudly alone does not reconsider the method

rst31-v2-r2-found-a-statistics.title: Do not move percentages into a different explanation
rst31-v2-r2-found-a-statistics.text: The text revised in 2021 mentions at least 90% in its food-poisoning classification explanation and 80% in a passage about employees and norovirus. Do not assume a common population or substitute these for current rates of all food poisoning. Do not invent unverified survey years, subjects, denominators or definitions. Understand preventive actions; when current rates are needed, check the conditions of that survey.

rst31-v2-r2-found-q001.objective: Keep historical percentages within their context.
rst31-v2-r2-found-q001.stem: An old text mentions at least 90% and 80% in separate explanations. How should training materials handle them?
options: Guess and add missing survey years or denominators
Check each context and survey conditions, leave unverified information unguessed, and do not declare current rates
Compare them as figures from the same population
Use 80% as the current employee-related share of all food poisoning
rst31-v2-r2-found-q001.explanation: Do not mix percentages from different contexts. State limits when timing, subjects or denominators are unverified; do not generalize to the current whole.
reasons: Do not add guessed information as fact
It preserves contextual limits without turning unknowns into facts
A common population has not been verified
It extends an old context to all current food poisoning

rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q001.objective: Distinguish the two historical cooling stages.
rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q001.stem: Which sequence matches the old text’s US cooling example? This is not a universal current rule.
rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q001.explanation: The historical example is at most 21°C within 2 hours, then at most 5°C within another 4 hours. Check current applicability separately; do not mix limits.
reasons: This matches the two stages described in the source.
The final temperature has not reached 5°C or below.
The times for the two stages are reversed.
The temperature sequence is reversed.

rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q002.objective: Do not treat examples of host fish as a safety list.
rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q002.stem: A purchased fish is absent from the Anisakis examples. What follows solely from its absence?
options: Its viscera may be served raw
Necessary checks still cannot be omitted
Heating is unnecessary
There is no risk
rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q002.explanation: The species are examples, not a safety guarantee. Absence does not remove preparation or necessary freezing/heating checks.
reasons: Absence does not authorize serving raw viscera.
It distinguishes examples from a safety guarantee.
Absence does not establish that heating is unnecessary.
Absence does not establish safety.

rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q003.objective: Classify each component by its actual process.
rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q003.stem: 1 = no heating; 2 = heat and serve; 3 = heat, cool and reheat. Classify, in order: main dish heated today and served immediately, sauce heated and cooled yesterday then reheated before serving, raw garnish.
rst31-v2-r3-hyg-q003.explanation: The main dish is 2, yesterday’s heated/cooled sauce is 3, and raw garnish is 1. Trace each component separately.
reasons: The processes for the main dish, sauce and garnish are all incorrect.
The processes for the sauce and raw garnish are reversed.
The processes for the main dish and sauce are reversed.
All three processes are correctly distinguished.

rst31-v2-r4-hyg-q001.objective: Match each problem with its corrective action.
rst31-v2-r4-hyg-q001.stem: Actions: A return/exchange; B investigate abnormal fridge temperature and adjust settings/request repair; C clean again and sanitize/disinfect as appropriate; D no food-handling work; E repeat correct handwashing. Match, in order: damaged packaging, abnormal fridge temperature, dirty utensils, dirty toilet, digestive symptoms, insufficient handwashing.
options: A→B→D→C→C→E
B→A→C→C→D→E
A→B→C→C→D→E
A→B→C→C→E→D
rst31-v2-r4-hyg-q001.explanation: Receiving defects require return/exchange; temperature abnormalities require checking cause and equipment. Clean and sanitize/disinfect utensils or toilets appropriately; stop food work for digestive symptoms and repeat inadequate handwashing. Heating does not automatically rescue every temperature-abused food.
reasons: A/B/C/C/D/E≠A/B/D/C/C/E
A/B/C/C/D/E≠B/A/C/C/D/E
A/B/C/C/D/E＝A/B/C/C/D/E
A/B/C/C/D/E≠A/B/C/C/E/D

rst31-v2-r4-hyg-q002.objective: Link date, check item, problem and action in the record.
rst31-v2-r4-hyg-q002.stem: R = receiving; W = handwashing; × = a recorded failure. On 5/8 (8 May), damaged packaging was found and exchanged. On 5/9 (9 May), missed handwashing after the toilet was found and repeated correctly. Which record links dates and items without hiding failures?
options: Mark all items good on both days, without notes
5/8:W×;5/9:R× + notes for each date
Combine them in next month’s unchecked cells
5/8:R×;5/9:W× + notes for each date
rst31-v2-r4-hyg-q002.explanation: Record the actual date and item, with the observed problem and action in notes. Exchange or repeated washing does not erase the failure found. Never prefill unchecked dates.
reasons: Do not omit a discovered problem after correction.
Swaps the items for 5/8:R and 5/9:W.
Use the actual date/item; do not fill unchecked cells.
Correctly links 5/8:R and 5/9:W.

rst31-v2-r5-ops-q001.objective: Calculate the relationship between cost ratio and gross margin using the same sales denominator.
rst31-v2-r5-ops-q001.stem: The cost ratio is 32%, based on sales for the same period. What is the gross margin?
rst31-v2-r5-ops-q001.explanation: With the same sales denominator, the two percentages total 100%. Thus 100 − 32 = 68%.
reasons: 100 − 32 = 68%, the remaining share of the same sales.
This repeats the cost ratio instead of giving the gross margin.
The ratios must add to 100%; adding 32 to 100 uses the wrong relationship.
0.68 is the decimal proportion, equivalent to 68%.

rst31-v2-r5-ops-q002.objective: Divide one dish's standard cost by its selling price and express it as a percentage.
rst31-v2-r5-ops-q002.stem: A dish has a standard cost of 240 yen and a selling price of 800 yen. What is its individual standard cost ratio?
options: About 333.3%
rst31-v2-r5-ops-q002.explanation: Use the dish's standard cost ÷ its selling price × 100: 240 ÷ 800 × 100 = 30%.
reasons: 70% is the gross margin under these conditions, not the requested cost ratio.
Dividing price by cost reverses the numerator and denominator.

rst31-v2-r5-ops-q003.objective: Divide the sales-quantity-weighted monthly standard cost by sales for that month.
rst31-v2-r5-ops-q003.stem: In one month, 30 portions of dish A (standard cost 200 yen) and 20 portions of dish B (standard cost 300 yen) were sold. Sales for these two dishes were 40,000 yen. What is the monthly standard cost ratio?
rst31-v2-r5-ops-q003.explanation: Monthly standard cost is 200 × 30 + 300 × 20 = 12,000 yen. Divide by sales for the same month and two dishes: 12,000 ÷ 40,000 × 100 = 30%.
reasons: The amount 12,000 yen cannot simply be read as 12%.
30 + 20 = 50 portions is a sales quantity, not a 50% ratio.
Add standard cost multiplied by quantity, then divide by the relevant sales for the same month.
The decimal 0.3 equals 30%; multiplying by 100 a second time is unnecessary.

rst31-v2-r6-ops-q001.objective: Calculate customers per staff-hour while accounting for service differences.
rst31-v2-r6-ops-q001.stem: A full-service restaurant served200customers with40staff-hours on the same day. Which calculation and judgment are appropriate?
options: 5customers/staff-hour. Consider time spent on table service; a lower figure than a different service model does not alone prove inefficiency.
200customers/staff-hour. Judge by customer count without staff-hours.
5customers/staff-hour. A lower figure always means inefficiency, whatever the service model.
0.2customers/staff-hour. Divide staff-hours by customers.
rst31-v2-r6-ops-q001.explanation: 200÷40＝5customers/staff-hour. Table service takes labor time, so figures from different service models cannot alone establish good or bad efficiency.
reasons: Uses customers÷staff-hours and considers time needed for service.
Without staff-hours as the denominator, this is not customers per staff-hour.
The calculation is right, but the service difference is ignored.
The numerator and denominator are reversed. Divide customers by staff-hours.

rst31-v2-r6-ops-q002.objective: Calculate cumulative sales share and apply the stated ABC practice bands.
rst31-v2-r6-ops-q002.stem: Same-period sales: X50,000yen, Y30,000yen, Z20,000yen. Sort by descending sales. For this exercise, cumulative share at row end≤70%isA,>70%to90%isB,>90%isC. What are Y’s cumulative share and category?
options: 100%, C. Use the total for every product as Y’s cumulative share.
30%, A. Use Y’s individual share as its cumulative share.
80%, B. These are exercise bands; a business may use different bands.
80%, A. The second-ranked product is A regardless of cumulative share.
rst31-v2-r6-ops-q002.explanation: Total sales are100,000yen. Through Y, cumulative sales are50,000＋30,000＝80,000yen, or80%; this is B under the exercise bands. Bands vary by business.
reasons: 100%is cumulative through Z, not through Y.
30%is Y’s individual share, not the cumulative share from X.
Adds X and Y, divides by the total and applies the stated bands.
80%exceeds the exercise’s A band. Rank alone does not set the category.

rst31-v2-r7-ops-a-voucher-timing.title: Giving a voucher to encourage the next visit
rst31-v2-r7-ops-a-voucher-timing.text: Give a next-visit voucher when settling the current bill, as a reason to return. For example, show it after the meal at checkout and explain that it is for the next visit. Distinguish this purpose from handing it out at the entrance merely to reduce today’s bill. Avoid automatically applying a next-visit voucher to the current bill.

rst31-v2-r7-ops-q001.objective: Choose when and why to hand out a next-visit voucher.
rst31-v2-r7-ops-q001.stem: A voucher campaign aims to encourage the next visit. Which handoff and explanation fit that aim?
options: Give it on entry and automatically discount today’s bill.
Give it at checkout but say it can always be used on this bill.
Do not give the voucher; only mention it after the guest returns.
Give it at this visit’s checkout and explain that it is for the next visit.
rst31-v2-r7-ops-q001.explanation: For this campaign, give and explain the voucher when settling the current bill to encourage a return. This differs from merely reducing today’s bill on entry.
reasons: This substitutes an on-entry same-day discount for the next-visit aim.
The timing matches, but the explanation wrongly changes next-visit use into current use.
It omits the checkout handoff and the invitation to return.
Both checkout timing and the purpose of a return visit match.

rst31-v2-r7-ops-q002.objective: Choose how to remember regular guests and thank them while maintaining quality.
rst31-v2-r7-ops-q002.stem: A restaurant wants to maintain its relationship with frequent guests. Which response is appropriate?
options: Maintain food quality, remember faces and preferred seats, and thank guests for visiting.
Assume remembering a face allows food quality to fall.
Decide today’s order from an old preference without asking.
Assume frequent guests do not need thanks.
rst31-v2-r7-ops-q002.explanation: Maintain quality while remembering regular guests’ faces, preferred dishes and seats, and expressing thanks. Remembered preferences do not decide today’s choice for the guest.
reasons: Combines maintained quality, remembering preferences and thanks.
Remembering a face does not justify lower quality.
This replaces remembering preferences with imposing today’s choice.
Express thanks to guests who return frequently too.

rst31-v2-r7-ops-q003.objective: Distinguish QSC experience from new visits generated by recommendations.
rst31-v2-r7-ops-q003.stem: A first-time guest liked the QSC, wants to return and recommended the restaurant to a friend. Which explanation correctly separates the two paths?
options: A good experience guarantees both the guest and friend will visit.
A recommendation only affects repeat visits by existing guests.
A good experience may encourage that guest to return; a recommendation may introduce a new guest.
The guest’s return and recommendation have no relation to QSC experience.
rst31-v2-r7-ops-q003.explanation: Improving the whole QSC experience can encourage a first-time guest to return. Their word-of-mouth recommendation can also create an opportunity for a new guest to visit. Neither guarantees a visit.
reasons: It changes a possible visit into a guarantee for everyone.
The friend receiving the recommendation may be a new guest who has not visited.
Separates the original guest’s return from a new guest’s opportunity to visit.
It ignores how QSC experience can prompt returns and recommendations.

rst31-v2-r8-ops-a-models.title: Rules and calculation assumptions at this practice restaurant
rst31-v2-r8-ops-a-models.text:
At this practice restaurant, next-visit vouchers cannot be combined with points; check the expiry printed on the voucher before use. These are store settings, not nationwide rules.
For one delivery order: sales2,000yen−food700−container100−delivery fee400＝800yen remaining. Other expenses are excluded, so this is not the whole restaurant’s final profit.
At this practice restaurant, do not reveal individual visit history to companions or third parties while greeting guests. Refer necessary disclosure requests to the manager. Consent and legal exceptions require separate consideration; this does not declare every conversation illegal.

rst31-v2-r8-ops-q001.stem: The practice voucher says “cannot combine with points; see voucher expiry.” Which guidance is correct?
options: Say combination is always allowed at every restaurant nationwide.
Say it never expires despite the printed expiry.
Ignore this voucher and promise combination is allowed.
Explain no combination and checking the printed expiry before use.
rst31-v2-r8-ops-q001.explanation: Follow this store’s no-combination and expiry settings. Other stores may differ.
reasons: Mistakes a store setting for a nationwide rule.
Changes a stated expiry into unlimited use.
Contradicts this voucher’s no-combination condition.
Explains both stated conditions.

rst31-v2-r8-ops-q002.objective: Subtract stated costs and respect the amount’s scope.
rst31-v2-r8-ops-q002.stem: One order: sales2,000yen, food700, container100, delivery fee400. Subtract only these three expenses. Which amount and explanation are correct?
options: 1,200yen: omit the delivery fee and call it final profit.
800yen: final profit after every expense, including rent.
800yen: the remainder under these assumptions, not the restaurant’s final profit.
1,600yen: do not subtract food or container costs.
rst31-v2-r8-ops-q002.explanation: 2,000−700−100−400＝800yen. Only these three expenses are subtracted; rent and other expenses are outside this example.
reasons: Does not subtract the400yen delivery fee.
Claims uncalculated expenses were also deducted.
Both arithmetic and limited expense scope are correct.
Does not subtract food700yen and container100yen.

rst31-v2-r8-ops-q003.stem: This practice store does not reveal individual visit history to third parties while greeting guests. A companion asks about it. What should staff do?
options: Reveal history without conditions because you recognize the face.
Assume a companion automatically has the guest’s consent and disclose it.
Say all guest conversation is illegal, so nothing may be said.
Do not reveal it there; ask the manager about necessary action.
rst31-v2-r8-ops-q003.explanation: Follow this store scenario: do not reveal history there; refer necessary disclosure requests to the manager. Data-consent and exception checks are separate; not every conversation is illegal.
reasons: Recognizing a face does not justify unconditional disclosure.
Companion status alone does not establish the guest’s consent.
Confuses handling individual information with banning every conversation.
Follows this store rule and manager confirmation.

rst31-v2-coupon-checkout-20261103.title: When to hand over a return-visit coupon
rst31-v2-coupon-checkout-20261103.text: Hand over a discount coupon intended to encourage a return visit at register checkout. If it is handed out on arrival and applied to that day's bill, it becomes an immediate discount rather than a reason to return. In this exercise, the cashier hands it over during payment and explains that it is for the next visit.

rst31-v2-coupon-timing-q001.objective: Choose when to hand over a return-visit coupon.
rst31-v2-coupon-timing-q001.stem: A restaurant prepares discount coupons for the next visit. When should staff hand a coupon to the guest?
options: Immediately on arrival
When taking the order
During register checkout
When the kitchen starts cooking
rst31-v2-coupon-timing-q001.explanation: Hand over a return-visit coupon during register checkout. Avoid confusing an arrival-time handout with a discount for that day.
reasons: Hand it over at checkout, rather than on arrival.
Hand it over at checkout, rather than when taking the order.
This matches handing over a return-visit coupon at checkout.
Hand it over at the guest's checkout, rather than when cooking starts.
